questions.chapter: The College Landscape and Application Rounds
questions.question_text: For most students, about how long does the college admissions process run from start to finish?

options.A: About three months, from the first application deadline to May 1
options.B: About two years, from the start of junior year to the end of senior year
options.C: About fifteen months, from the summer before senior year to the fall after graduation
options.D: About six months, from the start of senior year to the last regular deadline

questions.explanation: The chapter describes the process as running from the summer before senior year to the fall after graduation, about fifteen months. It includes all six stages: build your list, test, apply, seek aid, decide, and enroll. The shorter options cover only the application stage and leave out financial aid, the final decision, and enrollment steps like housing and orientation. That length is why many students feel behind, but it also makes the process forgiving.

questions.chapter: The College Landscape and Application Rounds
questions.question_text: Which application round is binding, meaning you must enroll if you are admitted?

options.A: Restrictive Early Action
options.B: Early Decision
options.C: Early Action
options.D: Rolling admission

questions.explanation: Early Decision is the only binding round in the chapter: if you are admitted, you must attend and withdraw your other applications, and you may apply to only one college this way. Early Action and rolling admission are non-binding. Restrictive Early Action limits where else you can apply early, but it is still non-binding, so an admitted student can decline the offer and decide by May 1.

questions.chapter: The College Landscape and Application Rounds
questions.question_text: What happens on May 1 in the admissions timeline?

options.A: It is the most common deadline for Regular Decision applications
options.B: It is the national deadline for choosing one college and paying a deposit
options.C: It is the date when the Common App opens for the new year
options.D: It is the date when most regular admission decisions are released

questions.explanation: May 1 is the national deadline for choosing one college and paying a deposit. The other dates belong to different anchor points: the Common App opens August 1, most regular deadlines fall between January 1 and February 1, and most regular decisions arrive from mid-March to early April. Knowing these fixed points helps you see why the calendar is lopsided, with most work packed into August through January.

questions.chapter: The College Landscape and Application Rounds
questions.question_text: Iowa State University and the University of Iowa are both public research universities. Why is only the University of Iowa called the state's flagship?

options.A: A flagship is any public university that offers both master's and doctoral degrees
options.B: A flagship is the public university with the lowest in-state tuition
options.C: A flagship is the best-known and usually oldest public research university in a state
options.D: A flagship is the public university that enrolls the most students in the state

questions.explanation: A flagship university is the best-known and usually oldest public research university in a state, often carrying the state's own name. Every flagship is a public research university, but not every public research university is a flagship, which is why Iowa State does not qualify. Offering graduate degrees makes a school a research university, not a flagship. The chapter does not define flagships by tuition or enrollment size.

questions.chapter: The College Landscape and Application Rounds
questions.question_text: Why does the chapter recommend submitting an application a few days before the deadline?

options.A: The deadline means the college must receive it, and servers often slow down on deadline night
options.B: Colleges give extra points to applications that arrive before the deadline
options.C: Early submission automatically moves your application into the early round
options.D: Most colleges stop accepting applications several days before their posted deadline

questions.explanation: An application deadline is the time by which the college must *receive* your application, not the time you start submitting it. The chapter notes that the Common App's servers are slow on deadline night nearly every year, and that is the student's problem, not the college's. Submitting a few days early is the only reliable protection. The chapter does not say colleges award extra points for early arrival or close before the posted date.

questions.chapter: The College Landscape and Application Rounds
questions.question_text: A student is admitted to a private university through Restrictive Early Action. What was the trade-off of applying in that round?

options.A: The student agreed to submit the application before the school's priority date
options.B: The student agreed to skip comparing financial aid offers in the spring
options.C: The student agreed not to apply early to most other private colleges
options.D: The student agreed to enroll if admitted and withdraw all other applications

questions.explanation: Restrictive Early Action, also called Single-Choice Early Action, is non-binding, so an admitted student can still say no. In exchange for applying, the student agrees not to apply early to most other private colleges, though exact rules vary by school. Agreeing to enroll and withdraw other applications describes Early Decision, not REA. Because REA is non-binding, the student remains free to compare aid offers before May 1.

questions.chapter: The College Landscape and Application Rounds
questions.question_text: A college received 18,000 applications and admitted 2,700 students. What is its admission rate, and which selectivity band does it fall in?

options.A: 15 percent, in the most selective band
options.B: 6.7 percent, in the most selective band
options.C: 25 percent, in the selective band
options.D: 15 percent, in the highly selective band

questions.explanation: The admission rate equals students admitted divided by students who applied, times 100: 2,700 ÷ 18,000 × 100% = 15%. In the chapter's bands, 10 to 30 percent is highly selective, while the most selective band is under 10 percent. The 6.7 percent option divides the numbers the wrong way and misplaces the decimal. The 25 percent option is a miscalculation, and the selective band covers 30 to 60 percent anyway.

questions.chapter: The College Landscape and Application Rounds
questions.question_text: A college has a 15 percent admission rate. Why doesn't that mean a particular applicant has a 15 percent chance of getting in?

options.A: The rate only counts students who applied in the Regular Decision round
options.B: The rate measures the quality of the college rather than how hard it is to get into
options.C: The rate is reported only for out-of-state applicants at most universities
options.D: The rate describes the whole applicant pool, and each student's odds depend on their own record

questions.explanation: The chapter warns that an admission rate describes the whole applicant pool, not you. Your odds depend on how your academic record compares with the students the college actually admits. The rate measures selectivity, not quality, so that option reverses the chapter's point. The rate also covers all applicants, and the chapter notes it can differ by round and by program, which is another reason a single number cannot predict one student's chances.

questions.chapter: The College Landscape and Application Rounds
questions.question_text: What is rolling admission?

options.A: A system in which a college reviews applications as they arrive and sends decisions until the class is full
options.B: A system in which a college holds all applications until a single spring decision date
options.C: A system in which a college moves deferred early applicants into the regular round
options.D: A system in which a college admits every applicant who has a high school diploma

questions.explanation: Rolling admission means a college reviews applications as they arrive and sends decisions continuously, usually within a few weeks, until the class is full. It is non-binding and often has no single deadline, though many rolling schools set priority dates for scholarships or housing. Holding all applications for one date describes a round like Regular Decision. Admitting everyone with a diploma describes open admission, which is a selectivity level, not a review system.

questions.chapter: The College Landscape and Application Rounds
questions.question_text: A first reader notes that an applicant took all 3 AP courses her small rural high school offers and rates her academics highly. What does this note show about how admissions officers evaluate applications?

options.A: Officers read a student's record against what that student's own high school offers
options.B: Officers compare every applicant against the same fixed number of AP courses
options.C: Officers care more about the number of courses taken than the grades earned
options.D: Officers give extra credit to rural students regardless of their course choices

questions.explanation: Admissions officers are usually assigned a territory and know the high schools in it. They read your record against what your school offers, not against an ideal applicant. Three AP courses out of three offered is the maximum available, so the reader treated it as a demanding schedule. A fixed AP count would ignore that context. The note also cites her A/A- grades, so it does not suggest grades are ignored or that location alone earns credit.

questions.question_text: What is a school profile?

options.A: A list of the activities and honors a student earned during high school
options.B: A short essay the student writes describing their high school experience
options.C: A one- or two-page summary of a high school that the counselor sends with the transcript
options.D: A college's annual report of the test scores and GPAs of its enrolled students

questions.explanation: A school profile is a one- or two-page summary of your high school that your counselor sends along with the transcript. It lists the advanced courses offered, how GPA is calculated, whether the school ranks, and what a typical graduating class looks like. It gives the transcript context, such as showing that a school offers only four AP courses. A college's report of enrolled students' scores is the Common Data Set, not a school profile.

questions.question_text: Which of these courses is NOT one of the core academic courses colleges care about most?

options.A: Spanish III
options.B: Intro to Computer Science
options.C: U.S. Government
options.D: Chemistry

questions.explanation: The chapter lists five core subjects: English, mathematics, laboratory science, social studies, and world language. Chemistry is a lab science, Spanish III is a world language, and U.S. Government is social studies. Computer science is named in the chapter as an elective. Electives can strengthen an application, but they do not replace the core, and many colleges leave them out when they recalculate GPA.

questions.question_text: A college's middle 50% range describes which part of its students?

options.A: The half of admitted students who chose to submit test scores
options.B: The students who scored above the college's published minimum
options.C: The students between the 25th and 75th percentiles
options.D: The students between the 50th and 100th percentiles

questions.explanation: The middle 50% range is the span between the 25th and 75th percentile of a college's students on a measure such as GPA or test scores. It holds the middle half of the class. The 25th percentile is not a minimum, so a quarter of the class falls below the bottom of the range. The 50th to 100th percentile would be the top half, not the middle half.

questions.question_text: On the Common App's school report, who rates the rigor of a student's course selection compared with other students at the same school?

options.A: The student, in the additional-information section
options.B: The student's school counselor
options.C: The student's AP teachers
options.D: The student's admissions officer at each college

questions.explanation: The school counselor rates the rigor of your course selection on the school report, using a five-step scale from "most demanding" down to "less than demanding." Selective colleges pay close attention to that rating because the counselor knows what courses were actually available to you. Admissions officers use the rating and the school profile to judge rigor, but they do not fill out the school report. Teachers write recommendations, not the rigor rating.

questions.question_text: Why do many colleges recalculate an applicant's GPA instead of using the one printed on the transcript?

options.A: High schools differ in scale and in which courses count, so colleges put grades on common rules
options.B: Recalculating lets colleges include senior-year grades before they are earned
options.C: Colleges want to add extra points for every honors and AP course taken
options.D: High school GPAs are often reported incorrectly by counselors

questions.explanation: GPA is less standard than it looks. High schools use different scales, treat pluses and minuses differently, include different courses, and may add weighting. To compare applicants fairly, many colleges keep only core courses from certain grades and put every school's grades on the same scale. The chapter does not suggest transcripts are usually wrong. Recalculation often removes weighting and electives rather than adding points.

questions.question_text: What most distinguishes holistic review from simply ranking applicants by their numbers?

options.A: Readers ignore grades and focus mainly on essays and recommendations
options.B: Readers add up separate ratings into a single total score for each applicant
options.C: Readers judge each applicant in context, asking what the student did with the opportunities they had
options.D: Readers consider only applicants whose test scores meet a set cutoff

questions.explanation: Holistic review evaluates the whole application and judges each applicant in context. Readers ask what a student did with the opportunities they had, not whether they are the best possible applicant. The academic record still comes first at most holistic colleges, so grades are not ignored. Reader ratings help committees compare files, but the chapter says they do not add up to a single score. Score cutoffs describe formula-based admissions.

questions.question_text: Using the Regent Admission Index (RAI = 3 × ACT + 30 × GPA + 5 × core years), what is the RAI for a student with a 23 ACT, a 3.50 GPA, and 16 years of core courses, and which threshold does it clear?

options.A: 249, clearing neither the resident nor the nonresident minimum
options.B: 254, clearing the resident minimum of 245 but not the nonresident minimum of 255
options.C: 244, falling just short of the resident minimum of 245
options.D: 259, clearing both the resident and nonresident minimums

questions.explanation: The calculation is (3 × 23) + (30 × 3.50) + (5 × 16) = 69 + 105 + 80 = 254. That clears the 245 minimum for Iowa residents but falls one point short of the 255 minimum for nonresidents. The other totals come from arithmetic slips in one of the three terms. Like the chapter's example of Casey, this student would be a clear admit as a resident but a borderline case as an out-of-state applicant.

questions.question_text: At a test-optional college, why might the published middle 50% ACT range be higher than the scores of all admitted students?

options.A: Test-optional colleges convert all SAT scores to higher ACT equivalents
options.B: Students who submit scores to test-optional colleges must meet a higher minimum
options.C: Test-optional colleges only report the scores of students admitted Early Decision
options.D: Only students who chose to submit are included, and they tend to have higher scores

questions.explanation: At test-optional colleges, the published test ranges include only students who chose to submit scores. Those students tend to be the ones with higher scores, which pushes the published range up. The chapter notes that a score near the bottom of such a range may be closer to the middle of all admitted students than the table suggests. The chapter does not describe special conversions, early-round-only reporting, or a higher minimum for submitters.

questions.question_text: Riley's GPA fell from 3.9 freshman year to 3.1 junior year because of a serious illness. What does the chapter suggest Riley do about it on the application?

options.A: Ask the counselor to remove the lower grades from the transcript
options.B: Make the illness the topic of every supplemental essay
options.C: Leave it out, since readers only look at the cumulative GPA
options.D: Explain the cause briefly in the application's additional-information section

questions.explanation: Readers look at the trend of grades over time as part of the academic record, so a falling trend makes a reader wonder what changed. If the decline had a cause, such as an illness, a family crisis, or a move, the chapter says the additional-information section is the place to explain it briefly. A reader cannot give context they don't know about. Readers do not look only at the cumulative number, and transcripts are official records the student cannot edit.

questions.question_text: According to the chapter, why does a rejection from a selective college often say more about that year's class than about the applicant?

options.A: The college is building a class to meet goals like filling majors, teams, and mission priorities
options.B: Selective colleges admit students mainly by formula and ignore the rest of the file
options.C: Selective colleges reserve most seats for legacy and donor applicants
options.D: Selective colleges reject most applicants at random once they meet a minimum

questions.explanation: Institutional priorities are the goals a college sets for each class, such as balancing majors, geographic reach, access, needed talents, and finances. An admissions office is building a class, not just picking the best individuals one at a time, so needs like string players or an under-enrolled major can decide close cases. The chapter calls the legacy claim a myth, and it does not describe selective admissions as random or formula-driven.

questions.question_text: For a final list of eight to twelve colleges, what mix does the chapter give as a common guideline?

options.A: 5–6 reach schools, 3–4 target schools, and 1 safety school
options.B: 3–4 reach schools, 3–4 target schools, and 3–4 safety schools
options.C: 2–3 reach schools, 4–6 target schools, and 2–3 safety schools
options.D: 1 reach school, 4–6 target schools, and 5–6 safety schools

questions.explanation: The chapter's guideline for a balanced college list is 2–3 reaches, 4–6 targets, and 2–3 safeties. Targets form the core because they are your most likely choices in April. A list heavy with reaches risks leaving you with no good options, while a list with almost no reaches gives up a shot at a stretch school. The chapter stresses that these numbers are not rules, but the principle is that at least one affordable college you'd love should be very likely to admit you.

questions.question_text: In the chapter, what is a dealbreaker?

options.A: A college trait that appears on every school's marketing materials
options.B: A condition a college must meet or you won't consider it at all
options.C: A reason a college might deny your application in the reading round
options.D: A priority you are willing to give up in exchange for a lower price

questions.explanation: A dealbreaker is a condition a college must meet or you won't consider it. Examples in the chapter include a student who must live at home to care for a sibling and a family that cannot pay more than a set amount. The chapter advises naming dealbreakers first because they remove schools from your list outright. A priority you would give up is a trade-off, the opposite of a dealbreaker.

questions.question_text: What tool is every college required by law to post on its website to estimate what a family will actually pay?

options.A: A school profile
options.B: A cost of attendance worksheet
options.C: A net price calculator
options.D: A Common Data Set

questions.explanation: Every college is required by law to post a net price calculator, which estimates your net price from your family's financial information. The chapter recommends using it for every college on your list early in your search, before you get attached. The cost of attendance is the price before aid, not an estimate of what you will pay. A school profile describes a high school, and the Common Data Set reports admissions data.

questions.question_text: According to the chapter, when do most four-year colleges require students to declare a major?

options.A: On the application, before admission
options.B: By the end of the first semester
options.C: Before the first semester of classes begins
options.D: By the end of the second year

questions.explanation: The chapter says most four-year colleges don't require you to declare a major until the end of your second year, which is why applying undeclared is common and fully accepted. Choosing a major on the application is required only for restricted or capped programs, such as some engineering or nursing programs. That exception is why an undeclared student who might want a capped major should check how those programs admit students before applying.

questions.question_text: What is the main difference between a personal priority and a simple preference?

options.A: Priorities have to be ranked, so you know which ones you'd give up to keep others
options.B: Priorities apply only to safety schools, while preferences apply to reaches
options.C: Priorities are set by parents, while preferences are set by students
options.D: Priorities only cover academic needs, while preferences cover social life

questions.explanation: The chapter says priorities differ from preferences in one important way: you have to rank them. Almost everyone would like a beautiful campus, great food, and a low price, but no college has everything, so the real question is which ones you'd give up to keep the others. Priorities can be academic, social, financial, or practical, so they are not limited to academics. They belong to the student and apply to every school on the list.

questions.question_text: The chapter compares academic, social, and financial fit to the legs of a stool. What point does this comparison make?

options.A: A college needs to match only two of the three to be a good choice
options.B: Financial fit matters only after academic and social fit are settled
options.C: Strong fit in one dimension doesn't make up for a failure in another
options.D: Social fit is the most important leg because it affects whether students stay

questions.explanation: A college has to work on all three dimensions of fit. A perfect academic and social match still falls over if the cost is out of reach, and an affordable school with a great program still isn't a fit if you'd be miserable living there. That is why two of three is not enough. The chapter treats the three legs as equally necessary rather than ranking one above the others or saving cost for last.

questions.question_text: Why are indirect costs easy for families to overlook?

options.A: They are usually covered in full by federal grants
options.B: They don't appear on the college's bill, even though you still pay them
options.C: They are paid only by out-of-state students
options.D: They are listed only after a student enrolls

questions.explanation: Indirect costs are expenses in the cost of attendance that the college doesn't bill you for: books and supplies, transportation, and personal expenses. Because they don't show up on the bill, they're easy to forget, but students still pay them out of pocket during the year. Every student has indirect costs, not only out-of-state students, though distance can raise them. They are part of the published cost of attendance, so they are listed before enrollment.

questions.question_text: According to the chapter, which is a harm caused by the no single right school myth?

options.A: It encourages students to choose majors they aren't interested in
options.B: It can push families into Early Decision before they've compared costs
options.C: It makes students skip the net price calculator for private colleges
options.D: It leads students to apply to too many safety schools

questions.explanation: The no single right school myth is the belief that one "dream school" exists for each student. The chapter says it makes students pour their hopes into one college, often a highly selective one, turns every other acceptance into a consolation prize, and can push families into Early Decision commitments before comparing costs. The truth is that most students could thrive at many colleges. The chapter does not link the myth to applying to too many safeties.

questions.question_text: A family can pay about $30,000 a year. College X has a sticker price of $78,000 and an estimated net price of $27,000. College Y has a sticker price of $45,000 and an estimated net price of $38,000. Which conclusion fits the chapter's guidance?

options.A: College Y fits the budget better because its sticker price is lower
options.B: Both colleges fit equally, because net price calculators are only estimates
options.C: Neither college fits, because both sticker prices are above $30,000
options.D: College X fits the budget, because net price is what the family would actually pay

questions.explanation: Sticker price is the published cost before aid, while net price is sticker price minus grants and scholarships. College X's net price of $27,000 is within the family's $30,000, and College Y's $38,000 is not. Judging by sticker price would cut the wrong school, just as Priya almost cut Hillcrest College. The chapter says calculators give estimates, not promises, but they are accurate enough to keep you from making that mistake.

questions.question_text: A college admits 40% of applicants and has a middle 50% SAT range of 1250–1400. A student's SAT is 1230, just below the range, but their GPA is near the top of the college's GPA range. How should the student classify this college?

options.A: As a target leaning toward reach, placed in the more cautious category
options.B: As a target leaning toward safety, because the GPA outweighs the test score
options.C: As a clear reach, because any number below the range rules out a target
options.D: As a safety, because the admission rate is above 30%

questions.explanation: This mirrors the chapter's example of a student whose SAT falls just below a range while the GPA sits near the top. Most counselors would call it a target leaning toward reach, with the rest of the application deciding the outcome. The chapter's rule is that when a college falls between categories, you place it in the more cautious one. It isn't a safety, since that requires numbers above the 75th percentile, and the strong GPA keeps it from being a clear reach.

questions.chapter: Researching and Narrowing Your College List
questions.question_text: Who publishes the College Scorecard, and what kind of information is it strongest on?

options.A: The College Board, strongest on test-score ranges and admission rates
options.B: Each state's higher education board, strongest on in-state tuition
options.C: Each college's institutional research office, strongest on class sizes
options.D: The U.S. Department of Education, strongest on cost and outcomes

questions.explanation: The College Scorecard is a free website from the U.S. Department of Education. It reports standardized data for nearly every college that accepts federal aid, including average net price by family income, graduation rate, typical debt, and typical earnings. Its admissions data is thinner, so the chapter suggests pairing it with the Common Data Set, which each college publishes itself. The College Board runs the BigFuture search site, a third-party tool whose numbers often come from these sources.

questions.chapter: Researching and Narrowing Your College List
questions.question_text: Which organization does the chapter name as the one that runs large national college fairs?

options.A: The U.S. Department of Education
options.B: The College Board
options.C: The National Association for College Admission Counseling (NACAC)
options.D: The Common Application

questions.explanation: The chapter says NACAC, the National Association for College Admission Counseling, runs large national college fairs, while many high schools and regions hold their own. A college fair brings representatives from many colleges to one place, so it's an efficient way to discover new schools and meet the admissions officer who may read your application. The Department of Education runs the College Scorecard, and the College Board runs BigFuture, a search site.

questions.chapter: Researching and Narrowing Your College List
questions.question_text: How many colleges does the chapter say a long list usually contains?

options.A: Five to seven
options.B: Eight to twelve
options.C: Fifteen to twenty-five
options.D: Thirty to forty

questions.explanation: A long list is your first, broad list of colleges worth researching, usually fifteen to twenty-five schools. It should come from your priorities, stretch beyond familiar names, and span reaches, targets, and safeties. Eight to twelve is the size of the final college list, which you reach by narrowing the long list in deliberate passes. In the chapter's example, Marcus builds a long list of eighteen and narrows it to ten.

questions.chapter: Researching and Narrowing Your College List
questions.question_text: What habit does the chapter recommend for combining data tools and experience tools?

options.A: Use experience tools for cost questions and data tools for social fit
options.B: Use data to decide which colleges to look at, and experience to decide which feel right
options.C: Use experience tools first, then check only your favorite colleges' data
options.D: Rely on data tools alone, since experience tools are designed to recruit you

questions.explanation: Data tools, such as the College Scorecard and Common Data Set, answer questions about admission chances, cost, and outcomes. Experience tools, such as visits and student reviews, answer questions about culture and social fit. The chapter says you need both: data alone can make an unhappy fit look perfect, and experience alone can make you fall for a campus you can't afford. The option pairing experience with cost and data with social fit reverses each tool's strength.

questions.chapter: Researching and Narrowing Your College List
questions.question_text: Why does the chapter call the retention rate an early warning signal?

options.A: It measures how quickly the college fills its class under rolling admission
options.B: It shows whether first-years return, and it reacts faster than the graduation rate
options.C: It reports how many admitted students choose to enroll each year
options.D: It predicts which applicants will be placed on the waitlist

questions.explanation: The retention rate is the percentage of first-time, full-time first-year students who return for their second year. Students who leave after one year usually do so because of cost, academic difficulty, or poor social fit. Retention and graduation rates usually move together, but retention reacts faster, so a low retention rate can flag problems early. It measures students who return, not admitted students who enroll, and it has nothing to do with waitlists.

questions.chapter: Researching and Narrowing Your College List
questions.question_text: Why should a single dramatic student review be given less weight than other evidence?

options.A: Colleges write most of the reviews that appear on review sites
options.B: Reviews only describe students who transferred away from the college
options.C: Review sites remove most negative reviews before posting them
options.D: Reviews are unverified and self-selected, so very good or bad experiences are overrepresented

questions.explanation: Student reviews can reveal things marketing doesn't, but the chapter says they are unverified and self-selected. Students with very good or very bad experiences post far more often than everyone in between. That's why you should look for patterns across many reviews and give more weight to specific details than to general feelings. The chapter doesn't claim colleges write the reviews or that sites delete negative ones.

questions.chapter: Researching and Narrowing Your College List
questions.question_text: A student wants to know how many of a college's classes are small and how many are large. Which Common Data Set section should they check?

options.A: Section C, first-year admission
options.B: Section B, enrollment and persistence
options.C: Section I, faculty and class size
options.D: Section H, financial aid

questions.explanation: In the Common Data Set, Section I covers faculty and class size, including how many classes are small and how many are large. Section B covers enrollment, graduation, and retention. Section C covers first-year admission, including middle 50% ranges and demonstrated interest. Section H covers need-based and merit aid. Knowing the sections lets you compare colleges question by question, since every college uses the same format.

questions.chapter: Researching and Narrowing Your College List
questions.question_text: Jordan has one afternoon on a college campus after the official tour ends. Which step follows the chapter's advice for getting the most from a visit?

options.A: Ask a student in the library what they like least about the college
options.B: Retake the tour with a different guide to compare answers
options.C: Spend the time in the admissions office collecting brochures
options.D: Wait until getting home a week later to write down impressions

questions.explanation: The chapter advises going beyond the tour and talking to students who weren't assigned to talk to you. Asking a student what they like least often tells you more than the tour, because tour guides are trained, enthusiastic volunteers. A second tour or a stack of brochures gives you more of the college's own message. The chapter also says to take notes within an hour of leaving, since campuses blur together after a few visits.

questions.chapter: Researching and Narrowing Your College List
questions.question_text: While narrowing a long list, a student runs a net price calculator and finds that a famous university would cost far more than the family can pay. According to the three-pass process, what should happen?

options.A: Cut it in Pass 1, because it clearly fails a dealbreaker no matter how famous it is
options.B: Move it to the safety category, since cost does not affect admission
options.C: Keep it until Pass 2, then label it a reach to balance the list
options.D: Keep it until Pass 3, since the student might picture being happy there

questions.explanation: Pass 1 cuts on dealbreakers and fit. If the net price calculator shows a college is out of reach, the chapter says to cut it no matter how famous it is. Cutting on fit first means you never waste time classifying colleges that wouldn't work anyway. Pass 2 classifies the remaining schools and balances categories, and Pass 3 tests whether you could picture yourself happy there. A college you can't afford can never be a true safety.

questions.chapter: Researching and Narrowing Your College List
questions.question_text: College P has an 80% retention rate, a 40% four-year graduation rate, and a 78% six-year rate. College Q has a 92% retention rate, a 65% four-year rate, and a 75% six-year rate. Which conclusion does the data best support?

options.A: College Q's students are less supported, because fewer finish in six years
options.B: College P is the better value, because its six-year rate is higher
options.C: The two colleges are equivalent, because their six-year rates are close
options.D: At College P, many students take extra years, which adds cost, and more first-years leave

questions.explanation: College P's six-year rate looks solid, but the large gap between its four-year and six-year rates means many students take five or six years, which adds tuition and living costs. Its lower retention rate is also a warning sign that more first-years leave. Looking only at six-year rates hides these differences, so treating the colleges as equal misses the point. College Q's high retention and four-year rate suggest students stay and finish on time.

questions.question_text: How many colleges can a student add to a single Common App account?

options.A: Up to 30
options.B: Up to 20
options.C: Up to 12
options.D: Up to 10

questions.explanation: The chapter says you can add up to 20 colleges on the Common App, which is far more than most students need. Eight to twelve is the usual size of a final college list, not the platform's limit. The Common App is accepted by more than 1,000 colleges, and each member college still sets its own deadlines, supplements, recommendation requirements, and testing policies, so you'll see a separate list of requirements for each one.

questions.question_text: What are the three principles that getting organized rests on, according to the chapter?

options.A: One source of truth, visibility to the people helping you, and early buffers
options.B: Paper backups, a printed calendar, and one deadline per college
options.C: Daily checklists, color-coded folders, and weekly counselor meetings
options.D: Applying early, submitting test scores, and using the Common App

questions.explanation: The chapter names three principles. One source of truth means every deadline, document, and password has a single home. Visibility means a parent, guardian, or counselor can see the plan and catch a missed date. Early buffers means setting your own due dates a few days before the real ones, since portals crash and recommenders run late. The other options list tools or choices that aren't the chapter's organizing principles.

questions.question_text: Which source does the chapter say you should treat as the final word on a college's specific requirements?

options.A: The college's own admissions website
options.B: The college's page on the Common App
options.C: A third-party college search website
options.D: A friend who applied to the college last year

questions.explanation: College-specific requirements, such as extra essays, recommendations, testing rules, and portfolios, are found on the college's own admissions website, usually on a "first-year requirements" or "how to apply" page. The Common App lists each member's requirements, but the chapter says to treat the college's site as the final word because it's updated most directly. Policies change yearly, so a friend's experience last year can be out of date, as Priya's graded-paper example shows.

questions.question_text: Why does the chapter recommend using the same dedicated email address for every application and account?

options.A: Using one address lets your counselor send documents automatically
options.B: The Common App will only accept one email address per student
options.C: Colleges give priority to applicants with professional email addresses
options.D: Colleges match records partly by email, so one address keeps your file together

questions.explanation: The chapter says to use the same address everywhere because colleges match records partly by email. A dedicated address also keeps college messages from getting buried, and you keep access after graduation, unlike a high school account. The chapter says a professional address looks better to admissions officers, but it doesn't say colleges give applicants priority because of it. Counselors send documents through the platform, not through your email.

questions.question_text: Why should checking applicant portals be a regular part of your routine?

options.A: Colleges count each portal login as demonstrated interest
options.B: Portals are the only place colleges post their application deadlines
options.C: Missing or unmatched documents appear in the portal before anyone emails you, if anyone does
options.D: Portals close permanently once the application deadline passes

questions.explanation: The chapter says portals are where problems surface. A transcript that arrived but wasn't matched to your file, or a recommendation listed as missing, appears in the portal long before anyone emails you about it, if anyone does. That's why the chapter suggests checking about a week after each submission and again after each supporting document deadline. Deadlines belong in your tracker and come from the college's website, not only the portal.

questions.question_text: Which statement about independent counselors matches the chapter?

options.A: They are reliable if they promise admission to specific colleges
options.B: They are optional, and they never replace the school counselor, who still sends your official documents
options.C: They are required for students applying to highly selective colleges
options.D: They can submit your official transcript in place of your school

questions.explanation: An independent counselor is a private advisor a family hires and pays. The chapter says plainly that you don't need one to apply successfully, and that one never replaces your school counselor, who still sends your official transcript and school profile. The chapter warns families to be wary of anyone who promises admission to specific colleges. It also points out that many community organizations offer free counseling, especially for first-generation and low-income students.

questions.question_text: Alex's legal name is Alexander, but everyone calls him Alex. How should he enter his name when he creates his Common App account?

options.A: Enter whichever name is shorter, since colleges match files by email instead
options.B: Enter his legal name exactly as on school records, and list "Alex" as a preferred name
options.C: Enter "Alex" everywhere, since that's the name teachers know him by
options.D: Enter "Alex" on the Common App and "Alexander" only on financial aid forms

questions.explanation: The chapter says to use your legal name exactly as it appears on school records, test registrations, and financial aid forms, because mismatched names are a common cause of documents not being matched to your file. You can list a preferred name separately. Using different names on different forms creates exactly the mismatch the chapter warns about. Colleges match records partly by email, but not only by email, so the name still matters.

questions.question_text: A student's application is due November 15, and their personal due date is November 10. Following the chapter's two-reminder pattern, when should they set calendar reminders?

options.A: November 3 and November 9
options.B: November 1 and November 15
options.C: November 8 and November 14
options.D: November 10 and November 15

questions.explanation: The chapter suggests two reminders for each deadline: one a week before your personal due date, to start finishing, and one the day before, to submit. With a personal due date of November 10, that means November 3 and November 9. The other options build reminders around the real deadline instead of the personal due date, which removes the early buffer the chapter recommends.

questions.question_text: A college accepts both its own institutional application and the Common App. A student is already sending the Common App and a finished personal essay to six other colleges. Which choice does the chapter's reasoning support?

options.A: Submit both applications to show extra interest in the college
options.B: Use the institutional application, since it always requires an essay
options.C: Use the Common App, since adding one more college takes little extra work
options.D: Use the institutional application, since colleges prefer their own forms

questions.explanation: The chapter's Iowa example shows the trade-off. If a college is one of several on your list and you already have a Common App essay, the Common App is little extra work. If it were your only application, the shorter institutional application might be simpler. The chapter doesn't say colleges prefer their own forms or that you should submit both. Iowa's own application actually requires no personal essay for general admission.

questions.question_text: Which family arrangement best matches the chapter's description of the parent and family role?

options.A: A parent owns the tracker and submits applications to keep things on schedule
options.B: A parent chooses the final college once offers arrive
options.C: A parent rewrites the student's essays so they sound more polished
options.D: A parent gathers tax documents and reads essay drafts only when asked

questions.explanation: The chapter describes families as supporting, informing, and helping with specific tasks while the student leads. Parents usually provide financial information and complete parent sections of aid forms, and they read drafts if asked. Essays written by parents tend to sound like parents, and readers can tell, so rewriting takes the process away from the student. The student owns the tracker and makes the final choice, while family helps compare costs and offers.

questions.question_text: Which organization makes the SAT, and what is its total score range?

options.A: ACT, Inc., scored from 320 to 1520
options.B: The College Board, scored from 400 to 1600
options.C: The College Board, scored from 1 to 36
options.D: ACT, Inc., scored from 400 to 1600

questions.explanation: The SAT is made by the College Board and given digitally in the Bluebook app. Its two sections, Reading and Writing and Math, are each scored from 200 to 800, for a total of 400 to 1600. The 1-to-36 scale belongs to the ACT, which is made by ACT, Inc. The 320-to-1520 range belongs to the PSAT/NMSQT, the practice version of the SAT.

questions.question_text: In which grade can a high PSAT/NMSQT score qualify a student for National Merit Scholarship Program recognition?

options.A: 10th or 11th grade
options.B: 9th grade only
options.C: 11th grade only
options.D: 12th grade only

questions.explanation: The PSAT/NMSQT is usually taken at school in October of 10th or 11th grade, but the chapter says that in 11th grade only, high scorers can qualify for recognition and scholarships through the National Merit Scholarship Program, with cutoffs that vary by state. Taking it in 10th grade is still useful as a free diagnostic. The PSAT doesn't go to colleges, so a low score costs you nothing.

questions.question_text: What does the chapter say about test accommodations on score reports sent to colleges?

options.A: Accommodations appear only if the student used extended time
options.B: Accommodations don't appear on score reports sent to colleges
options.C: Accommodations are shown only to test-required colleges
options.D: Accommodations are listed so colleges can adjust the score

questions.explanation: Test accommodations, such as extended time, extra breaks, a reader, or a separate room, are offered by both the College Board and ACT for students with documented disabilities or medical needs. The chapter states that they don't appear on score reports sent to colleges. Students with an IEP or 504 plan usually request them through the school's testing coordinator, and they should start early because approval can take several weeks.

questions.question_text: Why does the chapter call it a myth that "test-optional" means scores no longer matter?

options.A: A submitted strong score can still help, and scores can matter for scholarships and programs
options.B: Test-optional colleges secretly penalize applicants who don't send scores
options.C: Test-optional colleges require scores from all applicants after the first round
options.D: Test-optional policies apply only to students who have never taken a test

questions.explanation: Test-optional means you get to choose whether a score is part of your application. A strong score you submit can still help, and a weak one you leave off won't hurt you. Scores can also matter for merit scholarships, specific programs, and colleges that have gone back to requiring them. The chapter says test-optional colleges review applications without scores fully, so there's no hidden penalty. Students who believe the myth may discover a scholarship cutoff too late to test.

questions.question_text: A test-blind college won't consider SAT or ACT scores for admission. Why might it still ask for scores after a student enrolls?

options.A: To decide whether to offer the student a spot off the waitlist
options.B: To recalculate the student's admission decision
options.C: To place the student in the right first math or writing class
options.D: To report the student's score in its Common Data Set

questions.explanation: The chapter explains that some test-blind colleges still use scores after enrollment, for example to place students in the right first math or writing class. That's why it suggests checking whether a test-blind college asks for scores once you've committed. Because the college doesn't look at scores for admission, they can't change the admission decision or a waitlist outcome. The University of California and Cal State systems are the best-known test-blind examples.

questions.question_text: What is the main purpose of keeping an error log during test prep?

options.A: To track which official practice tests you have already used
options.B: To record each practice test's total score over time
options.C: To prove to colleges how much you prepared for the test
options.D: To find the pattern behind your mistakes and turn it into a study plan

questions.explanation: An error log is a running record of every practice question you get wrong, noting the question type, why you missed it, and what you'll do differently. The chapter says it turns mistakes into a study plan, and that most students who review only their score miss the pattern behind it. After a few practice tests, you sort the log by type and reason. A log of total scores alone would hide that pattern, and colleges never see your log.

questions.question_text: A student's ACT section scores are English 30, Math 25, and Reading 28. What is the composite score?
questions.explanation: The ACT composite is the average of the core section scores, English, Math, and Reading, rounded to the nearest whole number. Here, (30 + 25 + 28) ÷ 3 = 83 ÷ 3 ≈ 27.67, which rounds to 28. The value 83 is the sum, which is how the SAT total works but not the ACT. Choosing 27 drops the decimal instead of rounding, and 30 is simply the highest section score.

questions.question_text: A test-optional college reports a middle 50% SAT range of 1200–1360. A student scored 1300, and no scholarship or program rules apply. Using the chapter's rule, what should the student do?

options.A: Withhold the score, because test-optional ranges are inflated
options.B: Submit the score, because it is at or above the estimated midpoint of 1280
options.C: Withhold the score, because it is below the 75th percentile
options.D: Treat it as a judgment call, because it is inside the range

questions.explanation: The chapter estimates the midpoint as halfway through the middle 50% range: (1200 + 1360) ÷ 2 = 1280. A score at or above the midpoint is a strength, so the rule is to submit. The judgment-call zone is only between the 25th percentile and the midpoint. Being below the 75th percentile isn't a reason to withhold. The inflated-range caution actually makes a score near the midpoint look stronger, not weaker.

questions.question_text: A student took the SAT twice. In March: Reading and Writing 620, Math 640. In October: Reading and Writing 660, Math 610. What is the superscore?
questions.explanation: Superscoring combines your highest section scores from different test dates into a new composite. The best Reading and Writing score is 660 from October, and the best Math score is 640 from March, so the superscore is 660 + 640 = 1300. The March total is 1260 and the October total is 1270, which are single-date scores. The value 1250 pairs the two lower section scores. Not every college superscores, so check each policy.

questions.question_text: Which student's situation meets all three of the chapter's conditions for a retest?

options.A: A student below a scholarship cutoff, with a weak section to study, and a test date before deadlines
options.B: A student who has already tested three times and has no new prep plan
options.C: A student whose score is above the midpoint at every college but who wants a higher number
options.D: A student with a weak Math section who plans to retest the week after their last deadline

questions.explanation: The chapter says to retest when your score is below the level that matters for an important college or scholarship, you have a specific way to improve, and there's time for another test date before deadlines. The fourth student meets all three. The first student's score already works everywhere. The second has no time for scores to count. The third has tested three times with nothing changed, and the chapter says two sittings are enough for most students.

questions.question_text: On what scale are AP exam scores reported?

options.A: 1 to 7
options.B: 1 to 36
options.C: 1 to 5

questions.explanation: AP scores run from 1 to 5, with 5 meaning "extremely well qualified" and 1 meaning "no recommendation." Scores are released in early July, and each college decides which scores earn credit. The 1-to-7 scale is used for IB course assessments, and 1 to 36 is the ACT scale. Many colleges give credit for a 4 or 5, and some for a 3.

questions.question_text: How is the IB Diploma scored, and what is the minimum needed to earn it?

options.A: Out of 45 points, with at least 24 needed along with other conditions
options.B: Out of 36 points, with at least 18 needed
options.C: Out of 5 points per subject, with at least 3 in each
options.D: Out of 100 points, with at least 60 needed

questions.explanation: The IB Diploma is scored out of 45 points: up to 7 for each of six subjects plus up to 3 for the core requirements. Students need at least 24 points, along with other conditions, to earn it. The core includes Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay, and Creativity, Activity, Service. Because results arrive in July after senior year, colleges use predicted grades from teachers when they make admission decisions.

questions.question_text: Who sends the mid-year report to colleges, and roughly when?

options.A: The school counselor, usually in January or February
options.B: The student, usually in December with early applications
options.C: The College Board, usually in July with AP scores
options.D: Each teacher, usually at the end of the school year

questions.explanation: The mid-year report is a form your school counselor sends to colleges, usually in January or February, with your first-semester senior grades. On the Common App, the counselor submits it directly, and most selective colleges require it. It arrives in time to affect decisions for regular-round and deferred applicants. The final transcript, sent after graduation, is a different document that confirms you finished the year as promised.

questions.question_text: Which statement about college credit earned in high school matches the chapter?

options.A: The most selective colleges grant the most credit for AP scores
options.B: Credit transfers the same way to every college that accepts AP or IB
options.C: The college you enroll at decides what credit it accepts, and placement isn't the same as credit
options.D: Credit should be the main reason for choosing your senior courses

questions.explanation: The chapter lists three facts about college credit in high school. The college you enroll at decides what it accepts, so the same record can earn very different amounts. Credit and placement aren't the same, since some colleges let you skip an intro course without giving credit hours. And the most selective colleges tend to grant the least credit, not the most. The chapter calls credit a bonus to check after admission, not a reason to choose courses.

questions.question_text: Why does the chapter warn students to take dual-enrollment grades seriously?

options.A: A low dual-enrollment grade cancels the student's high school diploma credit
options.B: Dual-enrollment grades are hidden from colleges unless they are A's
options.C: Dual-enrollment grades replace the student's high school GPA
options.D: The grade goes on a real college transcript permanently and may be counted later

questions.explanation: Dual enrollment means taking actual college courses while in high school, and the grade goes on a real college transcript permanently. A C stays on that college record and may be counted when you later apply to college or to graduate or professional school. Dual-enrollment grades don't replace your high school GPA and aren't hidden. The chapter also notes that many colleges want an official transcript from the college that granted the credit.

questions.question_text: According to the chapter, what is the realistic goal for dealing with senioritis?

options.A: Stop worrying about grades once you've been admitted in the spring
options.B: Work just as hard as in junior year until graduation
options.C: Drop a core course to free up time once applications are in
options.D: Don't check out completely: keep grades roughly steady and go easier on extras

questions.explanation: The chapter says the goal isn't to work as hard as you did junior year, but to not check out completely. Keep attending, keep turning in work, and keep your grades roughly where they were, while going easier on extras rather than the courses you committed to. Grades still matter after admission because every offer is conditional on finishing well. Dropping a core subject or easing off sharply can actively hurt an application.

questions.question_text: Using the common weighting system (+0.5 for honors, +1.0 for AP), what is the weighted GPA for a B in AP History, an A in Honors English, an A in regular Spanish, and a B in regular Physics, each worth 1.0 credit?

options.A: About 4.13
options.B: About 3.88
options.C: About 3.50
options.D: About 3.63

questions.explanation: With the weights added, the B in AP History counts as 3 + 1.0 = 4.0, the A in Honors English counts as 4 + 0.5 = 4.5, the regular A counts as 4.0, and the regular B counts as 3.0. The total is 15.5 points over 4 credits, or about 3.88. The unweighted GPA for the same grades would be 14 ÷ 4 = 3.50. The other options misapply the honors or AP weight.

questions.question_text: Jordan plans to study engineering and took two APs as a junior. Which senior schedule best follows the chapter's course selection strategy?

options.A: Only electives in engineering-related topics, dropping English and world language
options.B: No math or science, to leave time for applications
options.C: All five core subjects, with AP Calculus and AP Physics, plus one elective Jordan enjoys
options.D: Six APs in every subject the school offers, including two in history

questions.explanation: The chapter's strategy is to keep all five core subjects, go deepest in your strengths and intended major, match or raise your junior-year level, choose two to four rigorous courses that fit, and leave room for one course you genuinely want. A future engineer should take the hardest math and physics available. Six APs ignores the two-to-four guideline, and dropping math, science, or core subjects is one of the few choices that can actively hurt an application.

questions.question_text: Taylor has committed to a college and took a dual-enrollment course at a community college senior year. What does Taylor need to do about final transcripts?

options.A: Nothing, because the college already received the mid-year report
options.B: Tell the counselor which college Taylor committed to, and also send the community college's final transcript
options.C: Send the high school's final transcript to every college that admitted Taylor
options.D: Wait for the college to request the transcripts in the fall semester

questions.explanation: The final transcript goes from your high school, after graduation, to the one college where you'll enroll. Your job is to tell your counselor which college you've committed to and check your portal to confirm it arrived. If you took dual-enrollment courses, you also need to send the final college transcript from the college that granted the credit. The mid-year report doesn't replace it, and nearly every college requires the final transcript before your first semester.

questions.question_text: A student took four APs as a junior and plans a senior schedule with no APs and no math, despite planning to major in economics. How would a reader most likely interpret this schedule?

options.A: As a sign of strong focus on the student's intended major
options.B: As a break in the student's trend that also doesn't fit their story
options.C: As neutral, since senior courses aren't graded until after decisions
options.D: As a sensible way to avoid burnout during application season

questions.explanation: Readers look at a senior schedule for whether it continues the trend and whether it fits your story. Dropping from four APs to none breaks the trend, and an economics student dropping math sends a confusing message. Senior courses aren't neutral, because colleges see them as "in progress" when they read your application. Avoiding burnout means choosing two to four rigorous courses that fit, not easing off sharply, which the chapter says can actively hurt an application.

questions.question_text: On the Common App, how many activities can you list, and how long can each description be?

options.A: Up to 20 activities, with descriptions up to 50 characters
options.B: Up to 5 activities, with descriptions up to 250 characters
options.C: Up to 10 activities, with descriptions up to 650 words
options.D: Up to 10 activities, with descriptions up to 150 characters

questions.explanation: The Common App activities list holds up to 10 activities, and each description is limited to 150 characters, about one or two short lines. The position field allows 50 characters and the organization field allows 100. The chapter notes that you don't need to fill all ten slots, since many strong applicants list six or seven. Up to five entries is the limit for the separate honors section.

questions.question_text: How many entries does the Common App's honors and awards section allow?

options.A: Up to five
options.B: Unlimited
options.C: Up to ten
options.D: Up to three

questions.explanation: Honors and awards have their own section on the Common App, separate from activities, with room for up to five entries. For each, you list the honor, the grade levels, and its level of recognition: school, state or regional, national, or international. The chapter advises listing the most significant honors first. It also says an empty honors section isn't a red flag, especially for students whose time goes to work or family.

questions.question_text: What simple pattern does the chapter recommend for a strong activity description?

options.A: Feeling + reflection + lesson
options.B: Goal + challenge + plan
options.C: Action + specifics + result
options.D: Title + organization + dates

questions.explanation: A strong activity description follows the pattern of action plus specifics plus result. You lead with your strongest action verb, add a number or concrete detail, and end with the result or scope. Title and organization have their own fields, so repeating them wastes space. Reflection and lessons belong in essays, not a 150-character description that should read more like a headline than a paragraph.

questions.question_text: According to the chapter, what do colleges actually aim for instead of well-rounded applicants?

options.A: Applicants who list all ten activities across different categories
options.B: Applicants who hold leadership titles in at least three clubs
options.C: A class made up mostly of students with school-sponsored activities
options.D: A well-rounded class made up of students who each have depth in one or two things

questions.explanation: The well-rounded applicant myth says colleges want every student to do a little of everything. In reality, colleges aim for a well-rounded class of students who are each deeply committed to one or two things. A shallow list of ten activities usually reads as weaker than real depth in two or three, because breadth alone can look like résumé-padding. The chapter also stresses that jobs and family duties count as fully as school clubs.

questions.question_text: Why do readers often give little weight to expensive, prestigious-sounding summer programs?

options.A: Readers only consider summer activities listed as paid work
options.B: These programs take place outside the school year, so they don't count
options.C: Many of these programs simply admit anyone who can pay
options.D: Colleges cannot verify that students attended them

questions.explanation: The chapter says readers know that many prestigious-sounding summer programs admit anyone who can pay, so they don't weigh them heavily. Summers do count, because they show what you choose to do with unstructured time. A summer job, a free local program, a self-directed project, or family responsibilities can be just as meaningful. What matters is what you did and what came of it, as Marcus's ordering app shows.

questions.question_text: What is the real value of an activities resume, according to the chapter?

options.A: It serves as a master document that feeds your activities list, recommenders, essays, and interviews
options.B: It gives you a place to list activities you didn't actually do
options.C: It replaces the Common App activities list at most colleges
options.D: It is required by most colleges in place of the honors section

questions.explanation: An activities resume is a one- to two-page document with more detail than the application allows. It usually isn't submitted, though some colleges and scholarships accept one. Its real value is as a master document. You cut its fuller descriptions down for the Common App, recommenders use it to write specific letters, it reveals essay topics, and it serves as a reference for interviews. Ana's sibling-care entry shows one entry feeding three parts of an application.

questions.question_text: A student swims on the school team for a 14-week season and spends about 12 hours a week at practices and meets. What total yearly time does this imply, and how should it be reported?

options.A: 168 hours, reported as 3 hours per week for 52 weeks
options.B: 624 hours, reported as 12 hours per week for 52 weeks
options.C: 26 hours, reported as 12 hours per week plus 14 weeks
options.D: 168 hours, reported as 12 hours per week for 14 weeks

questions.explanation: Total hours per year equals hours per week times weeks per year, so 12 × 14 = 168 hours. The chapter says that for a seasonal activity, you use the hours during the season and the number of weeks it actually runs. Reporting 52 weeks would inflate the commitment. Spreading the hours thin across the whole year misrepresents a typical week. Adding the two numbers instead of multiplying them is simply a math error.

questions.question_text: Which revision of "Participated in fundraising for the animal shelter" best uses action verbs as the chapter describes?

options.A: "I really enjoyed fundraising because I love animals"
options.B: "Organized 3 bake sales; raised $1,200 for local animal shelter"
options.C: "Animal shelter fundraising participant and volunteer member"
options.D: "Was very involved in helping the animal shelter with fundraising"

questions.explanation: Action verbs such as organized and raised replace vague phrasing like "participated in" or "was involved in," and they show your role fast. The strong revision also adds specifics and a result, following the action plus specifics plus result pattern. The other options keep passive phrasing, use only nouns, or describe feelings instead of actions. The chapter also warns that verbs must be true, so "organized" works only if the student really did.

questions.question_text: Kai's activities include a part-time job (20 hours a week for 3 years, now a shift lead), a club joined this year (1 hour a week), and National Honor Society. Which activity should Kai list first?

options.A: The club, because it was joined most recently
options.B: National Honor Society, because it is school-sponsored
options.C: The part-time job, because it shows the most time, commitment, and responsibility
options.D: Whichever activity Kai entered into the Common App first

questions.explanation: Readers see activities in the order you enter them, so ordering signals what matters most. The chapter says to list your most significant activities first, those with the most time, longest commitment, most responsibility, or deepest meaning. A job that takes twenty hours a week usually belongs near the top. Recency and school sponsorship aren't reasons to move an activity up, and entering them in the order you thought of them is the mistake Marcus fixed.

questions.question_text: A student's club raised $5,000 through an event that a team of six planned together, with the student as one of two leads. Which description best balances measurable impact with honesty?

options.A: "Raised $5,000 for the club single-handedly through my event"
options.B: "Co-led 6-person team that planned event raising $5,000"
options.C: "Practiced event planning for about 100 hours this year"
options.D: "Participated in a club event; money was raised"

questions.explanation: Measurable impact answers what difference you made, and numbers like $5,000 show it clearly. But the chapter cautions that impact must be honest: don't take credit for a team's result as if it were yours alone. "Co-led 6-person team" shows the real role and the real result. Claiming sole credit is dishonest, the vague version hides the impact, and the hours-practiced version forces a number that doesn't show what changed.

questions.question_text: What are the word limits for the Common App personal essay?

options.A: A maximum of 250 words, with a minimum of 150
options.B: A maximum of 650 words, with a minimum of 250
options.C: A maximum of 1,000 words, with a minimum of 500
options.D: A maximum of 500 words, with no minimum

questions.explanation: The Common App personal essay has a maximum of 650 words and a minimum of 250, and the application box enforces the maximum. The chapter says 650 words is about a page and a third double-spaced, which leaves room for one story told well, not three told briefly. Most strong essays use roughly 550 to 650 words. It's fine to draft long and cut later, since many first drafts run 900 words or more.

questions.question_text: How many Common App essay prompts are there, and what does the last one allow?

options.A: Ten prompts, and the last asks about a topic that makes you lose track of time
options.B: Seven prompts, and the last asks about a background or identity
options.C: Five prompts, and the last asks about an obstacle or failure
options.D: Seven prompts, and the last allows any topic of your choice

questions.explanation: The Common App offers seven essay prompts, and prompt 7 allows any topic of your choice. The background or identity prompt is prompt 1, the obstacle prompt is prompt 2, and the lose-track-of-time prompt is prompt 6. The chapter stresses that the prompts are broad on purpose, so most good essays fit more than one, and prompt 7 exists for stories that don't fit the others neatly.

questions.question_text: Which three essay structures does the chapter say work well for most personal essays?

options.A: Five-paragraph, compare-and-contrast, and persuasive
options.B: Question-and-answer, list-based, and dialogue
options.C: Narrative arc, montage, and idea-driven
options.D: Thesis-driven, research-based, and chronological summary

questions.explanation: The chapter names three structures. A narrative arc tells one story mostly in order with a turning point. A montage connects several short scenes through a common thread. An idea-driven essay explores a question or idea using examples from your life. The chapter says a personal essay doesn't need the five-paragraph format from English class, and a personal essay isn't an academic paper proving a thesis with sources.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between revision and editing?

options.A: Revision happens after submission, while editing happens before
options.B: Revision reworks content, structure, and meaning, while editing makes sentences correct
options.C: Revision only shortens the essay, while editing adds new scenes
options.D: Revision is done by others, while editing is done by the writer

questions.explanation: Revision is rethinking and reworking a draft by changing its content, structure, focus, or meaning, not just fixing sentences. Editing makes sentences correct, looking at clarity, wordiness, and word choice. The chapter puts it simply: editing makes sentences correct, and revision makes the essay better. Both are the writer's job, and revision often includes cutting, but it can also add detail or new reflection, as Ana's five drafts show.

questions.question_text: Why does the chapter say a small moment essay often works well?

options.A: Small moment essays fit only prompt 7, which readers favor
options.B: 650 words is enough to render one moment vividly and reflect on it, and it can stand out
options.C: Short experiences are less likely to include personal details
options.D: Readers prefer essays that avoid any reflection

questions.explanation: A small moment essay zooms in on one brief, specific experience, then reflects on it to reveal something larger. The chapter says it works because 650 words is exactly enough to render one moment vividly and reflect on it, and because a small, true moment often stands out among essays about big events. Reflection is still essential, and small moments are full of personal detail. They also aren't limited to one prompt.

questions.question_text: Which set of qualities does the chapter say makes a good personal story?

options.A: Yours, specific, and revealing something about you
options.B: Dramatic, unusual, and focused on a major achievement
options.C: Recent, positive, and connected to your intended major
options.D: Short, funny, and focused on a family member

questions.explanation: A good personal story is yours, meaning only you could tell it this way. It's specific, grounded in particular moments rather than a summary. And it reveals a quality, value, or change in you that the reader wouldn't otherwise know. The chapter points out that drama, achievement, and uniqueness of experience are not on the list. Many students have cared for a sibling or worked at a restaurant, and what makes a story distinctive is how you see it.

questions.question_text: Which opening line works best as an opening hook, according to the chapter's advice?

options.A: "The night our power went out, I finished my brother's science project by flashlight and learned what a circuit really was."
options.B: "Webster's Dictionary defines perseverance as continued effort despite difficulty."
options.C: "Since the dawn of time, humans have wondered how the world works."
options.D: "In this essay, I will describe how I became interested in science."

questions.explanation: The strongest hooks start in a scene, raise a question, or offer a striking detail. The first option drops the reader into a specific moment and makes them curious. The chapter lists dictionary definitions, sweeping statements like "since the dawn of time," and summaries of what the essay will say as the openings readers see constantly. A good hook doesn't have to be clever. It just has to be specific.

questions.question_text: A student wants feedback on a personal essay draft. Which approach follows the chapter's advice?

options.A: Ask one parent to rewrite the weaker paragraphs in a more polished style
options.B: Ask each reader only "Is it good?" so their answers are easy to compare
options.C: Ask two or three chosen readers specific questions such as "Where did you lose interest?"
options.D: Send it to eight readers and make every change they suggest

questions.explanation: The chapter says two or three readers are usually enough, since more brings conflicting advice. It recommends specific questions, such as what the essay says about you and where the reader lost interest, instead of "Is it good?" Above all, stay the author and treat feedback as information, not instructions. Having someone rewrite your essay costs your authentic voice and is dishonest, since the Common App asks you to certify the work is your own.

questions.question_text: A student has finished proofreading an essay in a word processor. What final step does the chapter recommend before submitting?

options.A: Rewrite the opening one more time to make it more dramatic
options.B: Submit it immediately, since the word processor already checked spelling
options.C: Run it through a thesaurus to replace common words with stronger ones
options.D: Paste it into the Common App box and read it there, since formatting can change

questions.explanation: The chapter says to paste the essay into the Common App box and read it there, because formatting such as italics, paragraph breaks, and special characters sometimes changes when you paste. You should also check the word count in the box itself and save the exact submitted version as "FINAL — submitted." Replacing words with thesaurus choices would hurt your authentic voice. Proofreading is the last pass for typos, not a time for new rewrites.

questions.question_text: Two students write about the same championship basketball game. One describes the winning shot. The other describes noticing, from the bench, that a teammate was hiding an injury. What does the chapter's test for overused topics suggest?

options.A: Both essays are equally strong, since they share the same prompt
options.B: Both essays should be dropped, since sports topics are forbidden
options.C: The winning-shot essay is stronger, since it describes the bigger moment
options.D: The bench essay is stronger, since only that student could have written it

questions.explanation: The big game is an overused topic because readers have seen thousands of winning shots. The chapter says overused topics aren't forbidden, but they need a fresh angle, such as an unexpected moment you noticed on the bench. Its test is that if a hundred students could write your essay with only the names changed, you need a more specific angle. The bench essay passes that test, while the winning-shot essay probably doesn't.

questions.question_text: How long are short-answer questions typically, according to the chapter?

options.A: 400 to 650 words
options.B: 250 to 400 words
options.C: 25 to 100 words
