If it's a hardship, the chapter says to ask the college about a deposit waiver or deferral, since many colleges waive or defer deposits for students with fee waivers or financial need. Iowa, for example, defers its acceptance fee to the first bill for students who used an application fee waiver. Skipping or paying late without approval can mean losing your place.

questions.question_text: A student has committed to one college but wants to stay on another college's waitlist. Which offers should the student decline?

options.A: The enrolled college's offer, to keep the waitlist option open
options.B: None, until the waitlist decision arrives in the summer
options.C: Every other offer except the enrolled college and that waitlist
options.D: Only the offers from colleges the student never visited

questions.explanation: Declining offers means formally telling every other college that admitted you that you won't attend, promptly after you commit. The chapter says that if you're staying on a waitlist elsewhere, decline everything except your enrolled college and that waitlist. Declining frees your place, and sometimes aid, for another student, possibly one on that college's waitlist. Holding offers until summer keeps seats others could use.

questions.question_text: A student weights Academic fit 5, Cost 4, and Social fit 3. College X scores 4, 3, and 5 on those factors. College Y scores 3, 5, and 3. What are the weighted totals?

options.A: College X 47, College Y 44
options.B: College X 12, College Y 11
options.C: College X 44, College Y 47
options.D: College X 60, College Y 60

questions.explanation: In a side-by-side comparison, you multiply each score by its weight and add. College X: (5 × 4) + (4 × 3) + (3 × 5) = 20 + 12 + 15 = 47. College Y: (5 × 3) + (4 × 5) + (3 × 3) = 15 + 20 + 9 = 44. The 12 and 11 totals add raw scores without weights, and the reversed option swaps the colleges. Even with X ahead, the chapter says to check which factors drive the gap before deciding.

questions.question_text: Jamie has decided to attend a college. Which set of steps completes accepting the offer the way the chapter describes?

options.A: Email the admissions officer and wait until August to submit any forms
options.B: Accept every loan offered, since aid can't be partly declined
options.C: Submit the intent-to-enroll form and deposit, accept the aid you want while declining unneeded loans, and tell your counselor
options.D: Pay the deposit and wait for the college to accept the aid on your behalf

questions.explanation: Accepting an offer means completing the intent-to-enroll form and paying the enrollment deposit through the applicant portal. At the same time, accept your financial aid through the aid portal, where you can accept grants and decline or reduce loans you don't need. Then save the confirmation and tell your counselor, since your school will send your final transcript there. Aid isn't accepted automatically, and you're never required to take every loan.

questions.question_text: A student admitted to two finalists can't afford to travel to either admitted student day. What does the chapter suggest?

options.A: Wait until summer orientation to visit both colleges
options.B: Choose the closer college, since visiting is required to enroll
options.C: Ask about travel grants, attend virtual events, and request a conversation with a current student
options.D: Skip comparing the colleges and decide by sticker price

questions.explanation: The chapter says many colleges offer virtual admitted student events, and some offer travel grants for admitted students with financial need, so ask the admissions office. If you can't revisit, attend a virtual event and ask to be connected with a current student in your intended major. Visiting isn't required to enroll. Waiting until orientation means committing first, and sticker price was set aside long ago in favor of net price.

questions.question_text: A student has five acceptances. One has a net price far above the family's budget, one admitted the student to a different program than intended, and three are affordable with strong fit. Which reasoning matches the chapter's narrowing step?

options.A: Remove the unaffordable college and weigh the different-program offer against direct-admit options before naming two or three finalists
options.B: Remove the affordable colleges first, since cost is the least important factor
options.C: Keep all five as finalists so no option is lost
options.D: Keep only the most selective college as the finalist

questions.explanation: The chapter says to narrow offers to two or three finalists that are affordable and that you'd be glad to attend. Remove any college that fails a dealbreaker or whose net price your family can't manage without unreasonable debt. Priya also cut a university that admitted her to general studies instead of English, since other offers admitted her to English directly. Keeping all five skips the narrowing, and selectivity isn't a reason to choose.

questions.question_text: Marcus asked the same three questions at both of his admitted student days. Why did that approach help him decide?

options.A: It turned two good feelings into a direct comparison on the factors he cared about
options.B: It let him skip writing down his impressions afterward
options.C: Colleges give extra aid to students who ask the same questions
options.D: It guaranteed both colleges would give identical answers

questions.explanation: Asking the same questions at each finalist, about intro class size and help, internships, and how aid changes, gave Marcus answers he could compare directly. The chapter says this turned two good feelings into a real comparison: Lakeshore had strong mentoring and internships, while Brookfield had small classes but fewer internships. The answers weren't identical, which was the point. The chapter still advises writing impressions down the same day.

questions.question_text: Riley must choose between College P, ranked higher nationally but costing $40,000 more over four years with a weaker program in Riley's major, and College Q, affordable with a strong program and a campus Riley loved on a revisit. Which judgment best reflects the chapter's reasoning?

options.A: College P, because a higher national ranking always outweighs cost and fit
options.B: College P, because the more expensive college must offer better outcomes
options.C: Neither, because Riley should wait for a waitlist offer instead of committing
options.D: College Q, because it wins on Riley's own priorities and a large cost gap usually isn't worth a higher ranking

questions.explanation: The chapter says to weigh offers by what matters to you, not by national rankings, and that a higher-ranked college isn't automatically the better choice. Cost, academic fit, social fit, and gut sense all favor College Q here, and Riley can explain the choice in a sentence. College P's only advantage is its ranking. Price doesn't prove better outcomes, and a waitlist is never a plan.

questions.question_text: What is a living learning community?

options.A: An online forum where admitted students find roommates
options.B: A student health plan offered to students who live on campus
options.C: A residence hall floor or building where students who share an academic interest or identity live together
options.D: A summer program that replaces orientation for first-year students

questions.explanation: A living learning community, or LLC, is a residence hall floor or building where students who share an academic interest or identity live together, often with linked courses, faculty involvement, and special events. Examples include communities for engineering, the arts, first-generation students, honors, or future teachers. The chapter says LLCs can help first-year students feel at home faster, and they often require a short spring application through the housing portal.

questions.question_text: Which subjects most often have placement tests, and when are they usually taken?

options.A: Only subjects without AP credit, usually after the first semester
options.B: Only English, usually as part of the housing application
options.C: Every subject in the major, usually during the first week of classes
options.D: Math, world languages, chemistry, and sometimes writing, usually online before orientation

questions.explanation: Placement tests help a college place new students at the right level, most often in math, world languages, chemistry, and sometimes writing. They're usually taken online before orientation. They don't affect admission, but they matter, since placing higher can save a semester and placing too high can mean struggling. AP scores and transfer credit may exempt you from some placement tests, so check first.

questions.question_text: Why does the chapter urge students to register for the earliest orientation date that works?

options.A: Course registration often happens at orientation, so a late date can mean popular sections are full
options.B: Early orientation dates come with a larger merit scholarship
options.C: Orientation is optional, so early dates are only for social events
options.D: Students who attend early orientation skip placement tests

questions.explanation: Orientation prepares new students for their first semester and typically includes advising, course registration, placement testing, and campus tours. The chapter stresses that orientation isn't optional and isn't just social. At many colleges it's where you register for first-semester classes, so a late orientation date can mean registering after popular sections fill. Placement tests are usually taken online before orientation, and orientation dates don't affect scholarships.

questions.question_text: Why should a family decide about health insurance before the college's waiver deadline?

options.A: Health insurance is required only for students in living learning communities
options.B: The waiver deadline is also the deadline for the housing application
options.C: Many colleges charge for their student health plan automatically unless it's waived by a deadline
options.D: Students without the college's plan can't move into housing

questions.explanation: Colleges require proof of health insurance or enrollment in the college's student health plan. The chapter says many colleges charge for their plan automatically unless you waive it by a deadline, so families keeping their own insurance need to act in time. Housing depends on health forms and immunizations, not on choosing the college's plan. The chapter doesn't tie insurance to living learning communities or to the housing application deadline.

questions.question_text: Kai committed in May, took three AP exams, and earned credit in a dual-enrollment course at a community college. What should Kai do so the credit counts before registration?

options.A: List the AP scores on the housing application instead of sending a report
options.B: Send only the AP scores, since dual-enrollment credit transfers automatically
options.C: Send an official AP score report, using the free send by June 20, and request the community college's official transcript
options.D: Wait for the college to request AP scores after the first semester begins

questions.explanation: AP credit transfer means getting AP, IB, and dual-enrollment credit recognized by your college. Send your official AP score report from the College Board, using the one free score send if you choose your college by June 20, and request an official transcript from the college that granted dual-enrollment credit. Then confirm in your portal how each was applied. Credit that hasn't posted by registration can mean signing up for a class you didn't need.

questions.question_text: A student's renewable scholarship requires full-time enrollment of at least 12 credits. While drafting a first-semester schedule, the student considers taking 10 credits to ease the transition. What does the chapter's advice suggest?

options.A: Plan at least 12 credits, with backup sections, to keep the scholarship
options.B: Skip registration until the scholarship office contacts the student
options.C: Take 10 credits, since scholarship rules don't apply in the first semester
options.D: Take 20 credits, to get ahead before any aid is checked

questions.explanation: The chapter says to keep scholarship and aid requirements in mind when registering, since many require full-time enrollment. A typical first semester is 12 to 16 credits, so planning at least 12 keeps the award while staying in a normal range. The chapter also advises drafting backup choices, since some sections fill. Dropping below 12 risks losing the scholarship, and an overloaded 20-credit schedule works against a balanced first semester.

questions.question_text: A student committed to the University of Iowa wants to choose a room online in June rather than be assigned one by staff. Which plan meets Iowa's requirements described in the chapter?

options.A: Wait to apply for housing until the final transcript is sent
options.B: Submit the housing application in August, just before On Iowa!
options.C: Schedule orientation first, then apply for housing in July
options.D: Finish the housing application by May 1 and schedule orientation by May 15

questions.explanation: The chapter says that at Iowa, students who finish their housing application by May 1 and schedule orientation by May 15 can choose their own rooms online in June, while students who apply later are assigned by staff. Earlier applicants also get earlier room selection times. Casey submitted the housing application in January, right after admission. Applying in July or August would miss the window, and housing doesn't wait on the final transcript.

questions.question_text: In July, Ana got a bill $1,800 higher than expected and briefly wondered whether to enroll at all. One call revealed a missing verification document had kept her state grant from posting. What does this example show about summer melt?

options.A: Most students who melt have changed their minds about college
options.B: Summer melt usually comes from small, fixable obstacles that feel like dead ends without help
options.C: Unexpected bills are a sign the college has withdrawn the student's aid
options.D: Students should wait for colleges to fix billing errors on their own

questions.explanation: The chapter says summer melt usually isn't a change of heart. It's a pile-up of small obstacles, such as a missed email, an unexpected bill, or a verification request, without a counselor nearby, since school is out. Ana's bill felt like a dead end but took ten minutes to diagnose. The grant hadn't been withdrawn, only delayed. The protection is to respond quickly and know who to call, rather than waiting.

questions.question_text: A student builds a roadmap for a private college that, unlike Iowa, requires the CSS Profile, two supplemental essays, and teacher recommendations. Using the capstone roadmap, what does the chapter suggest this student do?

options.A: Start over and relearn the process, since private colleges work differently
options.B: Keep the same sequence of steps, but find this college's version of each, such as its aid forms and supplements
options.C: Copy Iowa's roadmap exactly, since every college follows the same steps and deadlines
options.D: Skip the steps Iowa didn't require, since they are optional everywhere

questions.explanation: The capstone application roadmap applies the whole process to one real college. The chapter says the sequence doesn't change. Once you understand why each step exists, applying it to any college is a matter of finding that college's version of each step, not relearning the process. This college adds the CSS Profile, supplements, and recommendations that Iowa doesn't require. Copying Iowa's specifics would miss those, and the requirements aren't optional just because Iowa didn't have them.

questions.question_text: A student needs a college's housing deadline. A friend who enrolled last year says it's June 1, this book's example lists a different date, and the college's housing website for this year says May 15. Which source should the student rely on?

options.A: The friend, since they went through the process most recently
options.B: The book, since its facts were checked carefully
options.C: Whichever date is latest, to leave the most time
options.D: The college's website for the current year, recording the date and when it was confirmed

questions.explanation: Verifying current policies means checking each college's rules and deadlines for your own application year, not relying on last year's information, a friend's experience, or even a book. The chapter says policies change constantly, so confirm dates on the college's own website or studentaid.gov, email the office when in doubt, and record what you confirmed and when. Choosing the latest date could mean missing the real deadline and losing housing options.
